title: Algorithm visualizer
summary: A web app that animates sorting and pathfinding algorithms step by step, with playback controls and live counters.
why: It proves you understand algorithms well enough to show them, and that you can build a polished, interactive frontend. It also demos instantly: a reviewer sees your work in five seconds from a link.
brief:
Build a single-page web app that visualizes at least three sorting algorithms (for example insertion, merge and quick sort) and two pathfinding algorithms on a grid (BFS and DFS). Users generate random input, pick an algorithm, then play, pause, step forward and change speed while counters show comparisons and swaps, or cells visited.

The key design decision: write each algorithm as a pure function that returns a list of steps (or a generator that yields them) instead of mixing animation code into the algorithm. A renderer then replays the steps. This keeps the algorithms testable, makes stepping and racing easy, and is exactly the kind of separation of concerns interviewers like to hear about.

Constraints: TypeScript, with any framework you like (React, Svelte or none). Keep it accessible: keyboard controls, visible focus, and states that don't rely on color alone. Make it work on a phone, respect reduced-motion settings, and deploy it to a free static host so anyone can try it from a link.

milestones.title: Step model
tasks: Define a step format, for example { type: 'compare', i, j } and { type: 'swap', i, j }
Implement insertion sort as a function that returns steps
Write unit tests that replay the steps and check the result is sorted
milestones.doneWhen: Replaying insertion sort's steps on 100 random arrays always produces a sorted array, verified by tests.

milestones.title: Sorting view
tasks: Render bars with SVG or canvas from the current state
Add play, pause, step and a speed slider
Show live counters for comparisons and swaps
milestones.doneWhen: You can watch insertion sort on 30 bars, pause at any moment and advance one comparison at a time.

milestones.title: More sorting algorithms
tasks: Add merge sort and quick sort using the same step model
Caption each step in words, such as "Comparing 7 and 3: swap"
Show each algorithm's expected complexity next to the counters
milestones.doneWhen: On the same large random input, the counters show merge and quick sort making far fewer comparisons than insertion sort.

milestones.title: Pathfinding grid
tasks: A grid where users draw walls and place the start and the goal
BFS and DFS that return visit-order steps and the final path
Highlight visited cells and the path, and report the path length
milestones.doneWhen: A test confirms BFS finds the shortest path on several known grids, and on any maze BFS's path is never longer than DFS's.

milestones.title: Polish and deploy
tasks: Keyboard shortcuts and visible focus states
Deploy to a static host and put the link in the README
milestones.doneWhen: The live link works on a phone and a laptop, and every control can be used with the keyboard alone.

stretch: Dijkstra and A* on weighted cells
A side-by-side race between two algorithms on the same input
Shareable URLs that encode the array or the maze
rubric: A reviewer should see algorithms written as pure functions, separate from rendering, with unit tests
A reviewer should be able to run at least three sorts and two graph searches from a live link
A reviewer should see play, pause, step and speed controls that behave correctly mid-animation
A reviewer should see counters that match what the algorithm actually did
A reviewer should see keyboard access, reduced-motion support and states that don't rely on color alone
A reviewer should see a README with a GIF at the top and a short explanation of the step model
showcase: Put a GIF of one sort and of BFS at the top of the README, followed by the live link
Add a 'How it works' section with a small diagram: algorithm, then steps, then renderer
Feature the live link on your portfolio site and in LinkedIn's Featured section
resumeBullet: Built and deployed an interactive algorithm visualizer (TypeScript, React) for 5 sorting and pathfinding algorithms, using a tested step-recording model that separates algorithm logic from animation.
interviewTalkingPoints: Why the algorithms emit steps instead of animating directly, and what that made possible (tests, stepping, racing)
Why BFS guarantees the shortest path on an unweighted grid and DFS does not
How you kept large animations smooth (batching steps, requestAnimationFrame)
Accessibility decisions you made and why
